explanation: Assumption: `std::bind` is the standard tool for creating partial function applications and function wrappers, offering flexibility comparable to lambdas. Reality: While `std::bind` can achieve similar results, especially when binding arguments, lambdas offer significantly superior readability and clarity because they present the resulting function call in a standard, executable function body format. Why It Fails (for `std::bind`): `std::bind` relies heavily on positional placeholders (`std::placeholders::_1`, `_2`, etc.) which forces the reader to mentally map the placeholders back to the original function signature, obscuring which arguments are bound and which are passed through. Lambdas avoid this complexity by defining the resulting interface and logic directly.
practical_example: In a codebase using asynchronous callbacks, a developer uses `std::bind` to wrap a complex logging function, resulting in a line of code with five placeholders. Later, a maintenance programmer struggles to determine the actual signature required by the callback, requiring constant cross-referencing to the original function definition.
book: Effective Modern C++ by Scott Meyers
